title: Queue-aware scaling cost projections and SLO allocation
description: Spreadsheet-style working paper that translates request queue characteristics into GPU capacity and daily cost projections, with SLO allocation and cost tradeoffs between reserved vs. burst capacity. Intended to feed Optimize recommendations and product decisions on batching/queueing defaults.
summary: This draft captures a queue-aware capacity allocator: it converts end-user arrival patterns (short bursts, steady tail, weekend spikes) into instance-level GPU-hour needs and per-day cost estimates under different SLO targets (p50, p95, p99). It highlights how queueing/batching and a small burst pool can reduce unit cost without violating latency SLOs for most traffic. Contains worked examples, sensitivity rows, and pragmatic guardrails for rollout. NOT FINAL — numbers are an early estimate for a mid-size PLG customer profile.
key_assumptions: Avg tokens per request: 240 (mix of short prompts + context)
Tokens/sec per GPU (sustained, quantized runtime): 80k tokens/sec
Target utilization for steady instances: 0.55 (to keep latency predictable)
Burst pool uses pre-warmed instances with utilization 0.85 but limited concurrency
Cache/prefix hit rates vary by product; baseline assumed 12% effective token reduction
Queue element processing overhead (scheduling + batching latency): 8–15 ms per request on average
metrics_table: Row,Window,Requests/sec,P95 latency target(ms),Avg tokens/req,Effective tokens/sec (req * tokens),Cache hit %,Tokens/sec after cache,Tokens/sec per GPU,Instances needed,GPU-hours/day,Cost/day

calculation_notes: Instances needed = ceil((Requests/sec * Avg tokens/req * (1 - cache_hit)) / (Tokens/sec per GPU * target_utilization))
GPU-hours/day = Instances_needed * 24 (for always-on), for burst-only hours multiply by burst_duration_hours * instances
Round up rule: we always round up to nearest whole instance; use scale down cooldown 15m to avoid flapping
When P95 SLO is tight, add 10-25% headroom to Instances_needed as latency buffer depending on seq-length variance
scenarios: Scenario A - conservative reserved: reserve steady pool sized for workday-08-18 baseline + 25% headroom; burst pool small (2 GPUs) for short spikes; result: higher baseline daily cost but predictable latency

Scenario B - aggressive cost-minimize: smaller reserved pool (cover 60% baseline), rely on burst/spot for spikes with autoscaler; result: lower avg cost/day but P95 violations during rapid spikes unless batching is aggressive

Scenario C - SLO-centric: reserve enough capacity to meet p95 for 95% of 15-min windows, implement queue-based admission + degraded response paths for top 0.5% of requests; cost mid-range, predictable user experience
Sensitivity - cache improvement: +10 p.p. cache hit reduces tokens/sec demand by ~10% and can drop 1 GPU in baseline for mid-size workloads
raw_formula_examples: Example baseline calc: Instances = ceil((120 req/s * 240 tokens * (1 - 0.12)) / (80,000 tokens/s * 0.55)) => ceil(25344 / 44000) => ceil(0.576) => 1
Peak lunch calc: Instances = ceil((420 * 260 * 0.92)/(80,000 * 0.55)) => ceil(100464 / 44000) => ceil(2.28) => 3 (apply 15% headroom -> 3.3 -> 4 if strict)
Daily GPU-hours for 2 instances always-on = 2 * 24 = 48; cost = 48 * 2.85 = 136.8
recommendations: Default product config: start with conservative reserved pool sized to cover baseline workday with 15% headroom; enable small burst-pool (2-4 GPUs) for sub-5min spikes
Promote queue-aware batching in SDK: reporting of client-side instantaneous queue depth to server allows adaptive batching thresholds and reduces token cost per request
Expose a "cost profile" toggle in Console: conservative (reserved-heavy), balanced, or cost-optimized to let customers choose tradeoffs
Instrument per-route token distribution and sequence-length histogram; prioritize cacheable routes for aggressive caching policies
Run a 4-week A/B pilot: Balanced vs Cost-optimized on a subset of customers; track P95 latency, error rate, and daily GPU-hours
risk_and_uncertainties: Arrival pattern non-stationarity: sudden change in product behavior (e.g., feature launch) can invalidate estimates quickly
Cache effectiveness depends on client prompt diversity; optimistic cache assumptions overstate savings
Spot/market capacity for burst pools may not materialize in certain regions -> fallback to on-demand raises cost
Queue-based batching increases tail latency for some single-turn interactive flows if not tuned
